Theology. The philosophical and rational inquiry into the nature of God, divine revelation, and humanity's relationship to the divine. It is distinct from mere faith or religious practice. Theology attempts to understand religious claims through logic, reason, and argument rather than accepting doctrine on authority alone.

In the medieval period, scholasticism treated theology as the queen of sciences, applying rigorous philosophical method to religious questions. Thomas Aquinas exemplified this approach, arguing that reason and revelation are compatible, that they work together toward the same truth. He formulated the Five Ways, five rational arguments for God's existence based on observation of the natural world: through motion, causality, contingency, degrees of perfection, and design. This approach reconciled the rediscovered Aristotle with Christian doctrine, transforming theology into a systematic philosophical discipline.

But a central tension runs through all theology: the question of reason and faith. Can reason alone prove theological claims, or does religious knowledge rest on revelation that lies beyond reason's grasp? Natural theology seeks to prove God's existence through reason alone, without appeal to Scripture. Negative theology takes the opposite direction, arguing that God transcends all human categories and language, so we can only say what God is not, never what God is.

Leibniz's theodicy attempted to solve the problem of evil by claiming that this is the best of all possible worlds, though Voltaire famously ridiculed this solution. Modern theology confronts new challenges posed by science, history, and secular philosophy: how to ground religious authority in an age of critical inquiry. Process theology reconceives God as evolving alongside creation rather than immutable and all-powerful, seeking to resolve tensions between divine power and human free will.

Different religious traditions develop their own sophisticated theological systems. Christian, Islamic, Jewish, Buddhist, and Hindu theologies each grapple with ultimate reality and meaning in their own ways. Theology, at its heart, is philosophy applied to the deepest religious questions.
